chapter_title: A Decentralized Framework for Drug Assessment

scenes.title: The Wishonian Standard
scenes.narration_text: On Wishonia, we eliminated disease four thousand years ago. Every citizen has access to every treatment. Every outcome is recorded.
scenes.context: An alien perspective introduces the highly efficient medical system of planet Wishonia.

scenes.title: Simplicity of Trial
scenes.narration_text: Every disease gets studied. It's not complicated. You let sick people try things and write down what happens.
scenes.context: The narrator explains the simple logic of clinical observation used on their home planet.

scenes.title: The Instruction Manual
scenes.narration_text: But since your planet somehow hasn't figured this out, here's the instruction manual.
scenes.context: The narrator offers to guide Earth through its medical inefficiency.

scenes.title: The Participation Gap
scenes.narration_text: Out of two point four billion people with chronic disease, only one point nine million patients per year participate in trials annually.
scenes.context: A presentation of the staggering statistics regarding low clinical trial participation on Earth.

scenes.title: Unused Potential
scenes.narration_text:
That's zero point zero six percent.

Forty-four point eight percent would volunteer if they could.
scenes.context: The massive disparity between those who want to volunteer and those who actually can.

scenes.title: Systemic Barriers
scenes.narration_text:
Only zero point zero six percent currently participate.

This isn't because people don't want to help find cures.
scenes.context: Clarifying that the problem isn't lack of interest, but systemic design.

scenes.title: Hostile Design
scenes.narration_text: It's because your system was designed by someone who hates sick people.
scenes.context: A biting critique of how the current medical trial system treats patients.

scenes.title: Cost and Rejection
scenes.narration_text: Trials cost forty-one thousand dollars, require traveling to major medical centers, and reject eighty-six point one percent of actual patients.
scenes.context: Listing the financial and geographical barriers that prevent patient entry.

scenes.title: Inaccessible Care
scenes.narration_text:
You built a hospital you can't get into.
Impressive, (in a genocidal sort of way).
scenes.context: The narrator highlights the irony of a medical system that excludes those who need it most.

scenes.title: Safety Blindness
scenes.narration_text: Meanwhile, the system that's supposed to catch dangerous side effects misses ninety to ninety-nine percent of them.
scenes.context: Criticizing the massive failure rate in drug safety monitoring.

scenes.title: Reporting Failures
scenes.narration_text: Only one to ten percent of adverse drug events are ever reported to the F.D.A.
scenes.context: Data showing the minuscule percentage of drug side effects that reach regulators.

scenes.title: Data Void
scenes.narration_text: No denominator data. No effect sizes. No way to calculate how often a drug actually hurts people.
scenes.context: Explaining why current data is insufficient to assess drug safety for the general public.

scenes.title: The Suggestion Box
scenes.narration_text:
The safety monitoring system is a suggestion box that nobody uses.

You don't have a recruitment problem. You have a capacity problem.
scenes.context: Redefining the core issue of clinical trials as a lack of infrastructure, not a lack of people.

scenes.title: Medicine Defined
scenes.narration_text:
The Solution: Consumer Reports for Drugs.

On Wishonia, this is just called "medicine."
scenes.context: Introducing a transparent, data-driven approach used in advanced civilizations.

scenes.title: Social Medicine
scenes.narration_text: You type in what's wrong with you, see what worked for everyone else, and try it.
scenes.context: A user-friendly vision of how medicine could function with transparent shared data.

scenes.title: Automatic Records
scenes.narration_text: The outcomes get recorded automatically. We've had this for millennia.
scenes.context: Comparing Earth's manual systems to the automated recording of Wishonia.

scenes.title: Technological Lag
scenes.narration_text: You have all the technology to build it right now, and somehow haven't.
scenes.context: The narrator points out that Earth possesses the tools but lacks the implementation.

scenes.title: Open Protocols
scenes.narration_text: Your decentralized F.D.A. is an open coordination protocol. It connects companies with treatments to patients who need them.
scenes.context: Defining the 'Solution' as a protocol that bridges the gap between pharma and patients.

scenes.title: Internet of Medicine
scenes.narration_text: It's H.T.T.P. for clinical trials. A standard that lets all the existing systems talk to each other and share outcomes.
scenes.context: Using an internet metaphor to explain how medical data should be standardized.

scenes.title: Disconnected Data
scenes.narration_text:
You invented the internet over three decades ago and somehow forgot to plug medicine into it.

How It Works: Just Let People Try Stuff (Carefully).
scenes.context: The narrator highlights the absurdity of modern tech coexisting with archaic medical data silos.

scenes.title: Lessons of History
scenes.narration_text: Yes, the F.D.A. exists because patent medicine salesmen were literally poisoning people, and thalidomide gave "birth defect" a whole new meaning.
scenes.context: Acknowledging the dark history that led to current medical regulations.

scenes.title: Better Regulation
scenes.narration_text: Nobody's arguing for no regulation; we're arguing for regulation that doesn't kill more people than it saves.
scenes.context: A call for reform that prioritizes patient survival over bureaucratic inertia.

scenes.title: The Washington Thought
scenes.narration_text:
Here's a thought that apparently never occurred to anyone in Washington:

What if sick people could just... try treatments?
scenes.context: A simple, radical proposal to allow patient autonomy in treatment.

scenes.title: Observation Loop
scenes.narration_text:
And then we could... write down what happens?

And then other sick people could... see what worked?
scenes.context: Describing a virtuous cycle of experimentation and public record-keeping.

scenes.title: Rare Disease Void
scenes.narration_text: Your current system leaves ninety-five percent of rare diseases with zero approved treatments.
scenes.context: The failure of the current system to address the needs of rare disease patients.

scenes.title: Trial Barriers
scenes.narration_text: It bars over eighty-five percent of patients from the trials that might save them.
scenes.context: Stressing how current trial criteria exclude the very people who need a cure.

scenes.title: Healthy Test Subjects
scenes.narration_text: We've perfected a system where only the healthy and compliant test cures for the sick and desperate. It's genius, (in a suicidal sort of way).
scenes.context: The narrator mocks the practice of testing drugs on idealized rather than realistic patients.

scenes.title: Mythical Patients
scenes.narration_text: Trials are designed to test drugs on people who don't actually exist.
scenes.context: Criticizing the overly sanitized criteria used in clinical trial recruitment.

scenes.title: Comorbidity Exclusion
scenes.narration_text: To get into a study for an antidepressant, you can't have any other pesky problems like anxiety or P.T.S.D.
scenes.context: An example of how psychiatric trials reject complex, real-world patients.

scenes.title: Pristine Sick
scenes.narration_text:
You can't have a history of drug or alcohol use. You can't be on other medications.
You have to be the *perfect* kind of sick.
scenes.context: The narrator lists the 'perfect' requirements that make real patients ineligible.

scenes.title: Depression Disconnect
scenes.narration_text: The result? Only about fourteen percent of real-world patients with depression would actually qualify.
scenes.context: Highlighting the massive gap between trial participants and the actual patient population.

scenes.title: Messy Data
scenes.narration_text: The rest of us are too messy for their pristine, clean data.
scenes.context: A comment on how scientific purity often ignores the complexity of human life.

scenes.title: Tiny Groups
scenes.narration_text: On top of excluding everyone with a pulse, these "definitive" studies run on comically small groups.
scenes.context: Moving from the issue of who is tested to the issue of how many are tested.

scenes.title: Sample Size Irony
scenes.narration_text: They'll test a new heart drug on two hundred and seventy-five people.
scenes.context: Exposing the small sample sizes used to approve drugs for millions of people.

scenes.title: Statistical Risks
scenes.narration_text: A cancer drug on just twenty people. A diabetes drug on one hundred people. Then they prescribe the winner to millions.
scenes.context: Further examples of risky generalizations made from tiny clinical trial cohorts.

scenes.title: Kindergarten Stats
scenes.narration_text: You're basing survival on sample sizes smaller than kindergarten classes.
scenes.context: A stark comparison illustrating the inadequacy of current research scaling.

scenes.title: The Real Sick
scenes.narration_text: So instead of studying mythical, perfectly sick unicorns, what if you just collected data from everyone who's *actually* sick?
scenes.context: The narrator proposes shifting focus to real-world evidence gathering.

scenes.title: Real-World Evidence
scenes.narration_text: The Power of Real-World Evidence (Or: Spying on Sick People for a Good Cause).
scenes.context: The title slide for a new section on using global patient data to find cures.

scenes.title: The $500 Trial
scenes.narration_text:
Normal clinical trials: forty-one thousand dollars.

Oxford pragmatic trials: five hundred dollars.

That's not a typo.
scenes.context: Highlighting the extreme difference in cost per patient during the Oxford trial.

scenes.title: Introduction to RWE
scenes.narration_text: This framework is built on a slightly creepy idea: analyzing data from real patients in the real world.
scenes.context: The narrator introduces the core concept of the medical framework using Real-World Evidence.

scenes.title: Skeptics and Causation
scenes.narration_text:
Real-World Evidence (R.W.E.). A fancy term for "watching what happens."

Skeptics say, "Correlation isn't causation!"
scenes.context: Explaining RWE while acknowledging the primary criticism from medical skeptics regarding correlation.

scenes.title: The Failure of Old Research
scenes.narration_text: They say this while dying of diseases nobody bothered to study properly. They point to flip-flopping egg advice as proof this is voodoo.
scenes.context: A critique of how modern skepticism often results in stagnation while using inconsistent dietary advice as a weapon.

scenes.title: Confounding Factors
scenes.narration_text:
They're not wrong about the old way.
Old studies couldn't tell if eggs killed people or if egg-eaters just smoked three packs a day.
scenes.context: Describing the problem of confounding variables in traditional observational studies.

scenes.title: Personal Control Groups
scenes.narration_text: But now there's enough data and computing power to make each person their own control group. Track arthritis pain for a month.
scenes.context: The shift toward modern data processing where individual patients become their own comparison point.

scenes.title: Testing Turmeric Patterns
scenes.narration_text:
Take Turmeric, stop, start again. The pattern reveals whether it works or if it's coincidence.

A landmark meta-analysis in the
scenes.context: Using a simple example of N-of-1 testing to transition into larger academic proofs.

scenes.title: NEJM Meta-Analysis
scenes.narration_text: New England Journal of Medicine quietly ended this argument while nobody was listening. Researchers compared observational studies
scenes.context: Referencing a specific influential study that validated the observational approach.

scenes.title: Comparing Study Types
scenes.narration_text: against randomized controlled trials across nineteen different treatments. Cardiac surgery, cancer, ophthalmology, obstetrics.
scenes.context: Detailing the breadth of the NEJM study which looked at multiple medical fields.

scenes.title: Identical Effect Sizes
scenes.narration_text: The result: nearly identical effect sizes. The cheap method and the expensive method found the same answers.
scenes.context: Stating the shocking conclusion: cheap observation yields the same results as expensive trials.

scenes.title: Overpaying for Data
scenes.narration_text: You've been overpaying for data like tourists at an airport restaurant. On Wishonia, we figured this out about three thousand years ago.
scenes.context: A humorous comparison to illustrate the inefficiency of current medical spending.

scenes.title: The Pair of Dots
scenes.narration_text:
We call it "looking at what happened." You call it a "landmark meta-analysis."

Each pair of dots represents the same treatment
scenes.context: Visualizing the data comparison between the two different study methodologies.

scenes.title: Two Ways of Testing
scenes.narration_text: tested two ways: one observational (cheap, fast, real patients) and one randomized controlled (expensive, slow, cherry-picked patients).
scenes.context: Defining the contrast between the observational method and the standard clinical trial.

scenes.title: Overlapping Results
scenes.narration_text:
In nearly every comparison, the confidence intervals overlap.
Both methods found the same treatments work and the same treatments don't.
scenes.context: Confirming that statistical results remain consistent regardless of the testing cost.

scenes.title: Two-Stage Pipeline
scenes.narration_text:
The Two-Stage Pipeline: Watch First, Then Test.

Observational data finds the signals. But correlation still isn't proof (even you know that).
scenes.context: Introducing the structural solution for balancing speed and scientific rigor.

scenes.title: Stage One: Signal Detection
scenes.narration_text:
So the framework uses a two-stage pipeline:

Stage One (Signal Detection): Aggregate data from millions of patients.
scenes.context: Explaining the first step of the process which involves large-scale data collection.

scenes.title: Bradford Hill Criteria
scenes.narration_text: Score each treatment-outcome relationship using six Bradford Hill causality criteria: How strong is the effect? How consistent across people?
scenes.context: The scientific scoring system used to determine which observational signals are worth pursuing.

scenes.title: Timing and Dosage
scenes.narration_text:
Does the treatment come before the improvement? Is there a dose-response pattern?
Cost: approximately ten cents per patient.
scenes.context: Specific criteria for Stage One and its extremely low cost per patient.

scenes.title: Stage Two: Confirmation
scenes.narration_text: Stage Two (Confirmation): The top signals (the zero point one to one percent most promising) proceed to pragmatic trials embedded in routine care.
scenes.context: Explaining how the best signals are filtered and pushed into active testing.

scenes.title: Pragmatic Trial Costs
scenes.narration_text: Simple randomization. Real patients. Real conditions. Cost: approximately nine hundred and twenty-nine dollars per patient.
scenes.context: Defining the parameters and the specific cost of Stage Two pragmatic trials.

scenes.title: Eliminating Confounding
scenes.narration_text:
This eliminates confounding and proves causation.

Stage One filters millions of possibilities for almost nothing.
scenes.context: Synthesizing how the two-stage process yields high-certainty proof for a low price.

scenes.title: The Evidence Grade
scenes.narration_text: Stage Two confirms the winners for one forty-fourth the cost of traditional trials. The result: every treatment gets an evidence grade.
scenes.context: Comparing the massive cost savings and the final output of the pipeline.

scenes.title: Grading Definitions
scenes.narration_text:
Validated: Confirmed by pragmatic trial.

Promising: Strong observational signal, awaiting trial.

Signal: Hypothesis only, needs more data.
scenes.context: Listing the three specific categories treatments fall into under this framework.

scenes.title: Efficient Searching
scenes.narration_text: The cheap stage does the hard work of searching. The expensive stage only runs on candidates that deserve it.
scenes.context: Describing the division of labor between broad searching and focused confirmation.

scenes.title: Testing One vs. a Million
scenes.narration_text: Instead of spending fifty-seven million dollars testing one drug, you spend pennies watching a million treatments
scenes.context: A stark contrast in investment efficiency between traditional and pipeline testing.

scenes.title: Confirming Winners
scenes.narration_text:
and under a thousand dollars confirming the ones that work.

Proof It Works (While the F.D.A. Wasn't Looking).
scenes.context: Finalizing the cost argument and introducing a real-world case study.

scenes.title: The Oxford Recovery Trial
scenes.narration_text:
The Oxford Recovery Trial: How the British Accidentally Saved Medicine.

During COVID, while America was filling out forms,
scenes.context: Starting the narrative of how Oxford implemented this framework during the pandemic.

scenes.title: Testing on Dying People
scenes.narration_text:
Oxford University did something crazy. They just tested drugs on dying people to see if they stopped dying.

Cost per patient:
scenes.context: Describing the urgent and pragmatic approach taken by Oxford researchers.

scenes.title: Saving Lives with Steroids
scenes.narration_text:
Five hundred dollars. The cost of a nice dinner in Manhattan to save a human life.

Results:

Found that steroids cut COVID deaths
scenes.context: Relating the low cost to a tangible outcome: finding an effective treatment.

scenes.title: Massive Global Impact
scenes.narration_text:
by thirty percent.

Saved over one million lives globally.

Took three months instead of three years.

Cost less than one Super Bowl commercial.
scenes.context: Listing the staggering achievements of the Oxford trial in terms of lives, time, and money.

scenes.title: FDA Bureaucracy
scenes.narration_text: The F.D.A.'s response: "But did they file the correct paperwork?"
scenes.context: A final satirical note on regulatory resistance to efficient methodology.

scenes.title: Pragmatic Trial Success
scenes.narration_text: RECOVERY wasn't a fluke. A Harvard meta-analysis of one hundred and eight embedded pragmatic trials found median costs of just ninety-seven dollars per patient.
scenes.context: Discussing the surprisingly low costs associated with successful pragmatic clinical trials.

scenes.title: Large Scale Trials
scenes.narration_text: The Patient-Centered Outcomes Research network, or P.C.O.R.net, ADAPTABLE trial enrolled fifteen thousand and seventy-six patients across forty clinical sites
scenes.context: Referencing the massive enrollment numbers achieved in the PCORnet ADAPTABLE trial.

scenes.title: Cost Effective Models
scenes.narration_text:
at nine hundred and twenty-nine dollars per patient.

This model works across therapeutic areas, across countries, across decades.
scenes.context: Highlighting the versatility and cost-effectiveness of this clinical trial model across time and space.

scenes.title: Evidence Base Growing
scenes.narration_text: The evidence base for cheap, fast, embedded trials isn't one study. It's one hundred and eight and counting.
scenes.context: Emphasizing that pragmatic trials are backed by a substantial and growing body of evidence.

scenes.title: Simplicity of Pragmatic Trials
scenes.narration_text:
On most planets I've worked with, the pragmatic trial is the moment everyone looks at each other and says "wait, that's it?" Yes.
That's it.
scenes.context: Describing the common reaction to the refreshing simplicity of the pragmatic trial approach.

scenes.title: Sharing Results
scenes.narration_text:
You let sick people try things, write down what happens, and share the results.

What You'd See: F.D.A. dot gov two point zero.
scenes.context: Breaking down the core mechanics of a pragmatic trial and introducing the upgraded FDA portal concept.

scenes.title: FDA Site Upgrade
scenes.narration_text: The protocol upgrades F.D.A. dot gov from a digital cemetery to something useful. Cost: Less than one fighter jet that doesn't work.
scenes.context: Proposing a revamp of the FDA website to make it functional, using a military cost comparison.

scenes.title: The Search Box
scenes.narration_text:
Step One: Type in What's Killing You.

Revolutionary feature: A search box. The F.D.A.'s current website doesn't have this
scenes.context: Mocking the current lack of a simple search feature on the official FDA website for patients.

scenes.title: Seeing What Works
scenes.narration_text:
because they assume you've already died.

Step Two: See What Actually Works (Based on Reality, Not Theory).
scenes.context: Introducing a feature that shows treatment efficacy based on real-world data rather than theory.

scenes.title: Conditional Approvals
scenes.narration_text: Instead of "This drug is approved for exactly this condition in exactly these patients on exactly Tuesdays," you get:
scenes.context: Critiquing the overly specific and rigid conditions often attached to current drug approvals.

scenes.title: Realistic Outcomes
scenes.narration_text:
"Here's what happened to fifty thousand people who tried this:

Forty percent got much better.

Thirty percent got somewhat better.
scenes.context: Providing a statistical breakdown of how patients actually fared on a specific treatment.

scenes.title: Not Dying Consumer Reports
scenes.narration_text:
Twenty percent no change.

Ten percent grew a third nipple (but a useful one)".

It's like Consumer Reports, but for not dying.
scenes.context: Using humor to describe a user-friendly, transparent reporting system for medical treatments.

scenes.title: Ranking by Effectiveness
scenes.narration_text:
Treatment Rankings: Every Option, Ranked by Reality

Search any condition and see every treatment ranked by real-world effectiveness:
scenes.context: Visualizing a system where medical options are ranked by their actual success rates in the field.

scenes.title: Joining Phase Trials
scenes.narration_text:
F.D.A. Approved treatments with effectiveness scores from actual patients.

Phase three and Phase two trials you can join right now.
scenes.context: Describing how the new portal lists approved drugs alongside ongoing trials open for enrollment.

scenes.title: Experimental Options
scenes.narration_text:
Experimental options with preliminary data.

One-click access to join available trials.

No more guessing which treatment your doctor
scenes.context: Empowering patients to find and join trials with a single click, using real-time data.

scenes.title: Clear Treatment Rankings
scenes.narration_text: half-remembers from a conference. Just clear rankings based on what actually worked for people like you.
scenes.context: Advocating for data-driven decisions over anecdotal medical advice based on a doctor's memory.

scenes.title: Ending Failed Ideas
scenes.narration_text: The current system never publishes negative results. Humanity wastes billions repeating the same failed ideas.
scenes.context: Pointing out the massive waste caused by not publicizing unsuccessful clinical trials.

scenes.title: Remote Trial Access
scenes.narration_text:
Step three: Join a Trial from Your Couch (While Dying Comfortably).

Current system: Drive five hundred miles to a university hospital,
scenes.context: Contrasting the difficulty of current clinical trial logistics with a remote enrollment model.

scenes.title: Simplifying Participation
scenes.narration_text:
wait six months, get rejected for having the wrong kind of dying.

New system: Click button. Get pills. Report if you die.
scenes.context: Further detailing the streamlining of trial participation from the patient's perspective.

scenes.title: Fast Medication Delivery
scenes.narration_text:
Revolutionary!

Step four: Get Drugs Delivered Like Pizza (But More Life-Saving).

Amazon can deliver a banana costume in two hours
scenes.context: Highlighting the disparity between retail delivery speeds and the slow delivery of experimental drugs.

scenes.title: Fixing the Framework
scenes.narration_text:
but experimental medications take six months and require seven forms of I.D.?

Your framework fixes that.
scenes.context: Introducing a framework that removes the bureaucratic hurdles in medical research logistics.

scenes.title: Doctor as Researcher
scenes.narration_text:
Your pharmacy becomes a trial site. Your doctor becomes a researcher. Your dying becomes data.

Step five: Publish Results.
scenes.context: Envisioning a future where every part of the healthcare system contributes to research data.

scenes.title: Obsolete Report Forms
scenes.narration_text: Current system: five hundred-page case report forms that ask questions like "Rate your suffering on a scale of mauve to burnt sienna.".
scenes.context: Satirizing the complex and often irrelevant paperwork used in current clinical reporting.

scenes.title: Modern Results Reporting
scenes.narration_text:
New system:

"Are you dead?" Yes/No.

"If no, how dead do you feel?" Slider bar.

"Any new body parts?" Check all that apply.
scenes.context: Demonstrating how outcome reporting could be simplified to clear, essential questions.

scenes.title: Shared Patient Data
scenes.narration_text:
Step six: Everyone Benefits from Everyone's Suffering.

Your data helps the next person. Their data helps you.
scenes.context: Explaining the collective benefit of a data-sharing healthcare ecosystem.

scenes.title: Patient as Scientist
scenes.narration_text: Every pill becomes a tiny experiment. Every patient becomes a scientist. Every outcome gets recorded.
scenes.context: Proposing that all medical treatments should be treated as informative data points.

scenes.title: Outcome Labels Concept
scenes.narration_text:
You should have done this when you invented writing in three thousand B.C.

Outcome Labels: Nutrition Facts for Drugs.
scenes.context: Introducing the idea of Outcome Labels, comparing them to standard nutrition facts.

scenes.title: Labels vs Legal Inserts
scenes.narration_text: Food has nutrition labels. Cigarettes have warning labels. Drugs have... incomprehensible forty-page inserts written by lawyers having seizures.
scenes.context: Comparing standard product labeling to the legalistic complexity of current drug inserts.

scenes.title: Data Driven Summaries
scenes.narration_text: Outcome Labels fix that. Clear, data-driven summaries showing exactly what happens when real people try a treatment:
scenes.context: Explaining how Outcome Labels provide clear, honest data without marketing or legal jargon.

scenes.title: Real Patient Data
scenes.narration_text: No marketing spin. No forty-page legal disclaimers. Just clear data about what actually happens to people like you.
scenes.context: Describing the purity and relevance of the data provided by the proposed labeling system.

scenes.title: Depression Label Example
scenes.narration_text:
Here's what an Outcome Label for depression would actually look like:

OUTCOME LABEL: Depression Severity
scenes.context: Setting up a specific visual example of an Outcome Label for a common condition.

scenes.title: Large Participant Sample
scenes.narration_text: *Based on forty-seven thousand eight hundred and thirty-two participants*
scenes.context: Citing the extensive data pool used to generate the hypothetical Depression Severity label.

scenes.title: Rank One: Bupropion
scenes.narration_text:
Treatments Ranked by Effect Size

Rank one: Bupropion. Effect: negative twenty-eight point three percent.
scenes.context: The narrator introduces a list of treatments ranked by their clinical effectiveness.

scenes.title: Bupropion Data
scenes.narration_text: Sample size: two thousand eight hundred and forty-seven. Optimal dose: three hundred milligrams.
scenes.context: Specific data regarding the sample size and optimal dosage for Bupropion is provided.

scenes.title: Rank Two: Sertraline
scenes.narration_text: Rank two: Sertraline. Effect: negative twenty-four point seven percent. Sample size: five thousand one hundred and twenty-three.
scenes.context: The second-ranked treatment, Sertraline, is introduced with its effect percentage and sample size.

scenes.title: Rank Three: Venlafaxine Intro
scenes.narration_text:
Optimal dose: one hundred milligrams.

Rank three: Venlafaxine. Effect: negative twenty-one point two percent.
scenes.context: After detailing Sertraline's dose, the narrator moves to the third treatment, Venlafaxine.

scenes.title: Venlafaxine Data
scenes.narration_text: Sample size: one thousand eight hundred and ninety-two. Optimal dose: one hundred and fifty milligrams.
scenes.context: The specific study metrics for Venlafaxine are listed.

scenes.title: Equal Comparisons
scenes.narration_text: Every treatment ranked. Drugs, supplements, lifestyle interventions, off-label uses. All compared head-to-head using the same outcome data.
scenes.context: The narrator explains the methodology of comparing various types of interventions using uniform data.

scenes.title: The F.D.A.i.
scenes.narration_text:
No marketing budget required.

Your Personal Death-Prevention Assistant: The F.D.A.i.

On Wishonia, every citizen gets one of these at birth.
scenes.context: Introduction of the F.D.A.i., a fictional AI health assistant from the planet Wishonia.

scenes.title: Monitor and Adjust
scenes.narration_text: It monitors their health, finds treatments matched to their biology, and adjusts dosing in real time. We've had them for three thousand years.
scenes.context: Describing the long-standing use of continuous health monitoring technology on Wishonia.

scenes.title: Waste of Tech
scenes.narration_text:
You've had the technology for nearly two decades and used it to count steps.

Everyone gets a superintelligent doctor that lives in their phone
scenes.context: The narrator critiques Earth's underutilization of technology compared to the advanced AI doctor.

scenes.title: The AI Physician
scenes.narration_text:
and doesn't judge them for Googling "is my poop normal?".

The F.D.A.i. (Food and Drug Artificial intelligence) is like Siri,
scenes.context: A humorous look at the non-judgmental nature of the AI health assistant.

scenes.title: Survival Logic
scenes.narration_text:
but instead of telling you the weather, it tells you how not to die.

You: "I have diabetes and my foot fell off."
scenes.context: Comparing the AI's utility to common smartphone assistants through a hypothetical medical emergency.

scenes.title: Success Rates: Surgery
scenes.narration_text:
F.D.A.i.: "Based on fifty thousand similar cases, here's what worked:

Sixty percent success: Reattachment surgery plus Drug A.
scenes.context: The AI assistant provides statistical options for a medical issue.

scenes.title: Success Rates: Alternatives
scenes.narration_text:
Thirty percent success: Prosthetic foot plus Drug B.

Ten percent success: Hopping lessons plus Prayer.
scenes.context: Continuing the AI's breakdown of success rates for various diabetic foot treatments.

scenes.title: Success Rates: Essential Oils
scenes.narration_text: Zero percent success: Essential oils (but your remaining foot will smell lavender-fresh)".
scenes.context: The narrator highlights ineffective treatments listed by the AI's data.

scenes.title: Wearable Connection
scenes.narration_text: It connects to your wearables, apps, and medical records to find what's killing you while your doctor is still trying to remember your name.
scenes.context: Discussing the AI's speed and integration compared to traditional human doctors.
